title: India Just Broke Ground on Its Own Fifth-Generation Stealth Fighter Facility. The ₹15,803 Crore Bet Is on Home Soil.
excerpt: The AMCA flight test centre at Puttaparthi puts India's most ambitious indigenous combat aircraft programme on a physical foundation — and signals a strategic declaration that the country intends to test, certify, and fly its stealth fighter without foreign help.
body:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu laid the foundation stone on May 15 for the Aircraft Integration and Flight Test Centre of India's Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft programme at Puttaparthi, in Sri Sathya Sai district. The event marks the most tangible milestone yet in India's long quest to build an indigenous fifth-generation stealth fighter — a class of aircraft currently operated only by the United States, China, and Russia.

## The Scale of the Bet

The AMCA complex is estimated at ₹15,803 crore and will spread across nearly 650 acres. It is projected to generate approximately 7,500 high-skilled direct jobs over its lifecycle. The facility will serve as the primary hub for aircraft integration, development, and flight-testing — consolidating capabilities that India has historically depended on foreign testing ecosystems to provide.

The programme is being developed by the Aeronautical Development Agency under the Defence Research and Development Organisation. The first prototype is targeted for flight by 2028, with serial production planned for 2035. The AMCA is designed to eventually replace the Russian-origin Sukhoi Su-30MKI fleet and compete in the same class as the American F-35 and the Chinese J-20.

Alongside the AMCA centre, foundation stones were laid for a BDL Naval Systems Manufacturing Facility at Anakapalli, a Defence Energetics Facility and Ammunition Hub at Madakasira, and multiple projects under Drone City in Kurnool. Defence MoUs were exchanged between the Centre and the Andhra Pradesh government covering defence manufacturing, aerospace, and next-generation drone technologies.

## Andhra Pradesh's Defence Corridor Ambitions

The choice of Puttaparthi is strategic. Sri Sathya Sai district sits within striking distance of the Bengaluru aerospace corridor — including Kempegowda International Airport, HAL's facilities, and major defence establishments — positioning it as a natural southern extension of India's aerospace hub.

Under the state's Aerospace and Defence Policy 2025-30, Andhra Pradesh has identified six specialised clusters targeting naval systems, missiles and ammunition, unmanned systems, aerospace electronics, aircraft components, and defence R&D. The state already hosts investments from Bharat Electronics Limited, Bharat Dynamics Limited, and Kalyani Strategic Systems. The Rayalaseema region, long underserved in industrial investment, stands to be the primary beneficiary as the ecosystem takes shape.

"We cannot rely on others for our national security," Rajnath Singh said at the ceremony, framing the AMCA programme within the broader Aatmanirbhar Bharat push to reduce dependence on defence imports. India's defence production has hit ₹1.5 lakh crore over the past decade, but the country remains one of the world's largest arms importers.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora — particularly the sizeable NRI community of engineers, scientists, and defence professionals in the United States and Europe — the AMCA programme represents both pride and potential. India's aerospace ambitions have historically been viewed with scepticism by Western defence analysts, who point to decades of delays in the Tejas light combat aircraft programme as evidence that indigenous fighter development moves slowly.

But the AMCA is a different scale of commitment. The ₹15,803 crore investment, the 650-acre facility, and the explicit goal of eliminating foreign testing dependencies signal a level of institutional seriousness that the Tejas programme lacked in its early years. For NRI aerospace engineers working at Lockheed Martin, Boeing, Northrop Grumman, or Airbus Defence, the AMCA programme raises an increasingly plausible question: could there be a career path back home?

The Indian government has been quietly expanding outreach to diaspora defence professionals, and the growing sophistication of India's private defence sector — with companies like Tata Advanced Systems, Adani Defence, and L&T Defence entering fighter jet subsystem manufacturing — creates pathways that did not exist a decade ago.

## The Hard Questions

The harder question is timeline. India's fifth-generation fighter programme has been in development for over a decade, and a flight-test centre breaking ground in 2026 does not guarantee the aircraft flies on schedule. The engine remains the most critical technological gap — India does not yet have an indigenous fighter jet engine capable of supercruise, and negotiations with France's Safran for technology transfer have moved slowly.

What Puttaparthi does is remove one excuse. India now has a facility dedicated to testing its own stealth fighter. Whether the ecosystem — skilled workforce, supply chain, testing protocols — matures fast enough to match the ambition is the accountability test that will play out over the next decade.
